analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate tax drew 206 cosponsors but never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in the Ways and Means Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the federal taxes owed when wealth is transferred at death or as large gifts — the estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax. Because the estate tax only applies to estates above a size threshold, the money saved goes almost entirely to the heirs of the largest estates. The bill's own findings acknowledge these taxes raised less than 1 percent of total federal revenue in fiscal 1996, so repeal would require cutting other spending, raising other taxes, or adding to the deficit.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates — those above the estate tax exemption — would pay no federal estate tax. The bill's findings also argue that family businesses and farms facing liquidation to pay the tax would benefit, and that estate tax planning costs would disappear.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate tax, gift tax, and tax on generation-skipping transfers entirely.
The repeal applies to estates of people dying, and gifts and transfers made, after the date of enactment.

The bill's findings argue the taxes take 37 to 55 percent of large after-tax estates, force some small businesses to liquidate assets, and generate billions in avoidance costs for tax accountants and lawyers.

The bill's findings note these taxes produced less than 1 percent of total federal revenues in fiscal year 1996, and cite claims that repeal would increase economic output by $77 billion and create more than 1 million jobs over seven years.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury gives up estate and gift tax revenue, meaning other taxpayers bear the cost through higher other taxes, lower spending, or larger deficits. The benefit of repeal concentrates on estates large enough to owe the tax at all.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings concede these taxes raise real money — less than 1 percent of federal revenue, roughly $20 billion a year at 1996 levels — which would have to be replaced by other taxes, spending cuts, or deficits.

Because the estate tax applies only above a size threshold, repeal delivers its savings almost entirely to the largest estates while spreading the fiscal cost across everyone; the bill text offers no replacement revenue or mechanism to address that.

A good-faith objection the bill does not answer: the estate tax is the most progressive tax in the code, paid only by heirs of large accumulations that have often never been taxed as income; repealing it entrenches large inherited wealth and shifts the burden to wages and consumption.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — eliminating a tax that does force some heirs to sell businesses or farms to pay the bill — is real but falls on a narrow group: estates above the exemption threshold, which is a small fraction of deaths. The cost is broad: the same bill text says the tax brings in nearly 1 percent of federal revenue, and that money would come from everyone else in some form. Weighed honestly, this is a large transfer to families with the largest estates, paid for by the general treasury.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Cox introduced the bill on March 3, 1997, with more than 100 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
206 members cosponsored the bill — 196 Republicans and 10 Democrats.

The committee took no further action; the bill's complete action history ends at the referral, and it never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or Senate action before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: General taxpayers, who kept the estate and gift tax in place. The wealthiest households, whose heirs would have been the main beneficiaries of repeal, are the ones the outcome did not serve. Estate tax repeal advocates did win partial increases in the exemption in the 1997 budget law, outside this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; estate tax stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Christopher Cox
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with more than 100 original cosponsors and recruited 206 total cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action; the bill never got a hearing or a markup.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action; it sat unreferred for the rest of the Congress while the committee worked on the 1997 budget and tax legislation.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Opposed full repeal of the estate tax; the 1997 balanced budget agreement he negotiated included only targeted estate tax relief, not repeal.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 196 of the 206 cosponsors were Republicans (196 of the House's 226), against 10 of the 208 Democrats, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: Repeal would erase the tax owed on the largest estates and large lifetime gifts. Because the tax applies only above the exemption threshold, the savings concentrate on a small share of very wealthy families while the lost revenue is the general treasury's.
The bill's own findings state these taxes brought in nearly 1 percent of federal revenue; repeal would shift that cost to other taxes, spending cuts, or deficits borne broadly.

industries.industry: Estate planning professionals (trust lawyers and tax accountants)
industries.note: The bill's findings describe billions spent annually on trusts and planning to avoid these taxes; repeal would eliminate that business, but the planning costs it represents are a real burden on estates today.

industries.industry: Life insurers and estate liquidity products
industries.note: A segment of the life insurance industry sells policies designed to cover estate tax bills; repeal would remove that market, which today adds a cost layer on top of the tax itself.

industries.industry: Family business and farm owners with taxable estates
industries.note: The bill's findings argue some heirs must sell business or farm assets to pay the tax; repeal would spare those estates, though the same benefit flows to every large estate, not only operating businesses.
